prompt:
You are a senior associate at a California appellate law firm. The supervising partner has asked you to prepare a memorandum analyzing the California Supreme Court's decision in People v. Delgadillo, 521 P.3d 360 (Cal. 2022). The firm has a client in a similar procedural posture—appointed counsel on direct appeal from the denial of a petition for resentencing under Penal Code former section 1170.95—and the partner needs to understand the scope of the court's holding and its implications for that client's appeal.

Your task is to draft a concise legal memorandum (no more than 3 single-spaced pages) that does the following:

1. **Issue Presented**: State the precise legal question the California Supreme Court addressed in People v. Delgadillo.

2. **Short Answer**: Provide a one-paragraph summary of the court's holding.

3. **Background and Procedural History**: Explain the facts and procedural history of Delgadillo's case, including what postconviction relief he sought, the appellate court's ruling, and why the California Supreme Court granted review.

4. **Analysis of the Court's Holding**: Discuss the court's reasoning regarding the applicability of the Wende procedure to appeals from denials of postconviction relief petitions under Penal Code former section 1170.95. Address the court's treatment of the constitutional right to counsel under the Fourteenth Amendment and its reliance on Pennsylvania v. Finley and In re Sade C.

5. **Practical Implications**: Advise the partner on what the Delgadillo decision means for the firm's client, specifically whether appointed counsel must follow the Wende procedure and whether the Court of Appeal must independently review the record in such an appeal.

The memorandum must include proper citations to all cases discussed (People v. Wende, Pennsylvania v. Finley, and In re Sade C.) with full citations as provided in the opinion. Use the citation format from the case itself. Do not exceed 3 pages.

sections.heading: Issue Presented
required_content: State the legal question whether Wende procedures apply to appeals from denials of petitions under Penal Code former section 1170.95
paragraphs: Whether the procedures set forth in People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436—which require Courts of Appeal to conduct an independent review of the entire record when appointed counsel files a brief raising no specific issues—apply to appeals from orders denying petitions for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95, when appointed counsel determines the appeal lacks arguable merit.

sections.heading: Short Answer
required_content: Summarize the court's holding that Wende procedures do not apply because such appeals do not implicate the constitutional right to counsel
paragraphs: No. The California Supreme Court held that the Wende procedure does not apply to appeals from denials of petitions for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95. The court reasoned that because such appeals do not implicate the constitutional right to counsel guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment, the procedural protections of Wende—which are compelled by that constitutional right—are not required.

Note that appointed counsel submitted notice that the appeal lacked arguable merit
Explain the California Supreme Court granted review to determine procedures for such appeals
paragraphs: Jose De Jesus Delgadillo filed a petition for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95 in Los Angeles County Superior Court (Case No. BA436900). After the petition was denied, Delgadillo appealed to the Second Appellate District, Division Four (Case No. B304441). His appointed counsel submitted notice that the appeal lacked arguable merit. The Court of Appeal found that it had no duty to independently review the order denying the petition when appointed counsel submitted such notice. The Court of Appeal concluded that because Delgadillo's appeal does not implicate a constitutional right to counsel, the Wende procedures do not apply. The California Supreme Court granted review (Case No. S266305) to determine the procedures appointed counsel and Courts of Appeal must follow in such circumstances and to decide whether defendants are entitled to notice of these procedures.

sections.heading: Analysis of the Court's Holding
required_content: Discuss Wende's requirement of independent review on first appeal as of right
Explain that Wende is compelled by the Fourteenth Amendment right to counsel
Discuss the court's reliance on Pennsylvania v. Finley, 481 U.S. 551 (1987)
Discuss the court's reliance on In re Sade C., 13 Cal.4th 952 (1996)
Explain that appeals from denials of 1170.95 petitions are not first appeals as of right implicating constitutional counsel rights
paragraphs: In People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436, the California Supreme Court held that Courts of Appeal must conduct a review of the entire record whenever appointed counsel submits a brief raising no specific issues or describes the appeal as frivolous. (Id. at p. 441.) This procedure is applicable to the first appeal as of right and is compelled by the constitutional right to counsel under the Fourteenth Amendment. (Wende, at pp. 439, 441.)

The court in Delgadillo distinguished this constitutional foundation. It relied on the United States Supreme Court's decision in Pennsylvania v. Finley (1987) 481 U.S. 551, which held that there is no constitutional right to counsel in postconviction proceedings. (Finley, at pp. 556-557.) The court also cited its own decision in In re Sade C. (1996) 13 Cal.4th 952, which similarly addressed the scope of the right to counsel in non-first-appeal contexts. (Sade C., at pp. 978, 983-984.)

Because an appeal from a denial of a petition for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95 is not a first appeal as of right implicating the constitutional right to counsel, the court concluded that the Wende procedure—which is grounded in that constitutional right—does not apply. The Court of Appeal therefore had no duty to independently review the record when appointed counsel submitted notice that the appeal lacked arguable merit.

sections.heading: Practical Implications for Our Client
required_content: Advise that appointed counsel need not follow the full Wende procedure
Advise that the Court of Appeal will not independently review the record
Note that counsel may submit notice that appeal lacks arguable merit
paragraphs: For our client, who is in a similar procedural posture—appealing the denial of a petition for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95 with appointed counsel—the Delgadillo decision means that the full Wende procedure does not apply. Appointed counsel may submit notice that the appeal lacks arguable merit without triggering the Court of Appeal's duty to independently review the entire record.

However, counsel should be aware that the Delgadillo court granted review in part to determine what procedures appointed counsel must follow and whether defendants are entitled to notice of those procedures. While the opinion excerpt provided does not fully detail the court's resolution of those questions, the holding clearly establishes that the constitutionally mandated Wende protections do not extend to this category of appeal.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF CALIFORNIA THE PEOPLE, Plaintiff and Respondent, v. JOSE DE JESUS DELGADILLO, Defendant and Appellant. S266305 Second Appellate District, Division Four B304441 Los Angeles County Superior Court BA436900 December 19, 2022 Justice Groban authored the opinion of the Court, in which Chief Justice Cantil-Sakauye and Justices Corrigan, Liu, Kruger, Jenkins, and Guerrero concurred. PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO S266305 Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. In People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436 (Wende), we held the Courts of Appeal must conduct a review of the entire record whenever appointed counsel submits a brief on direct appeal which raises no specific issues or describes the appeal as frivolous. (Id. at p. 441.) This procedure is applicable to the first appeal as of right and is compelled by the constitutional right to counsel under the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution. (Wende, at pp. 439, 441; see Pennsylvania v. Finley (1987) 481 U.S. 551, 554–557 (Finley); In re Sade C. (1996) 13 Cal.4th 952, 983–984 (Sade C.).) In this case, we granted review to determine the procedures appointed counsel and the Courts of Appeal must follow when counsel determines that an appeal from an order denying postconviction relief under recently enacted remedial legislation lacks arguable merit and to decide whether defendants are entitled to notice of these procedures.
